title: Sent
tomorrow: who taught you your first prayer, and who will you teach?

segments.voice: Last week ended on the universal call: holiness is for everyone, addressed by name. The line was you, by name. Today, where that call sends you.
screen: `YOU, BY NAME.` → `WHERE THE CALL SENDS YOU.`

segments.voice: Car keys already out, someone checking the game score, a toddler escaping down the aisle. The end of Mass. And the last thing the priest says isn't goodbye. In the old Latin it's ite, missa est. Pope Benedict the Sixteenth wrote that missa first simply meant a dismissal, and in Christian use came to carry the sense of a mission. Go: you're sent. Now one man who took that literally. Paul, alone in Athens, walking a city full of temples and statues, waiting for friends to catch up. He stops at a small altar with an inscription on it.
screen: `CAR KEYS ALREADY OUT.` → `ITE, MISSA EST.` → `PAUL, ALONE IN ATHENS.`

segments.voice: Luke tells it in Acts. Paul is invited to speak at the Areopagus, and he doesn't open by telling Athens it's wrong. He opens with what he saw, in the Douay-Rheims: "I found an altar also, on which was written: To the unknown God." You already reach for this God, he says. Then he goes wider: God "hath made of one, all mankind, to dwell upon the whole face of the earth." One human family, Athenians included. He even quotes their own poets: "For we are also his offspring." Only then does he speak about Jesus and the resurrection. And Luke is honest about the result. Some laughed. Some said, we'll hear you again about this. A few believed, a man named Dionysius and a woman named Damaris among them. That's the scene the Church means by a missionary disciple. Pope Francis wrote that every baptized person is one: not a professional, not a salesperson. Someone who has met something good and is sent to share it, starting from what they hold in common with the person in front of them. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: Paul's speech to the philosophers of Athens opens with a compliment, a stranger's altar, and a line from a Greek poet.
screen: `TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.` · `OF ONE, ALL MANKIND.` · `SOME LAUGHED, SOME BELIEVED.` · `EVERY BAPTIZED PERSON IS SENT.` · then, large: `GO, YOU ARE SENT.`

segments.voice: Open a message to one person you care about, and write one true sentence about something that's given you peace, starting from something you both share. No pitch, no argument. Send it, save it, or delete it: the writing is the practice.
Missionary disciple. Pope Francis's name for every baptized person: someone who met something good and is sent to share it.
Pocket this one: go, you are sent, the way Paul started at a stranger's altar with what they shared. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: Mia asked why i still go to Mass if i'm leaving. i froze. how do i say it without preaching?
options: Start where Paul did, with what you two share. Then just say what it gives you.
Bring a few strong arguments, so you can answer anything she throws back.
Don't. Faith is private, and sharing it always comes off as preaching.
chat.meaning: Paul opened in Athens with the city's own altar and poets. Every baptized person is a missionary disciple: sent, gently, from common ground.

ite, missa est.meaning: Latin: go, it is the dismissal; the old closing words of Mass

Areopagus.meaning: a hill and council in Athens where Paul spoke

Acts.meaning: the Acts of the Apostles, Luke's book about the early Church

Dionysius.meaning: an Athenian council member who believed after Paul spoke

Damaris.meaning: an Athenian woman named among those who believed

notes: Acts 17:23, 17:26 and 17:28 quoted from Douay-Rheims (Challoner); confirm exact wording (DR prints the inscription in capitals: TO THE UNKNOWN GOD).
Sacramentum Caritatis 51 paraphrased: in antiquity missa simply meant dismissal; in Christian usage it gained the sense of mission. The claim is Benedict XVI's, attributed to him. Confirm.
Evangelii Gaudium 120 paraphrased: every baptized person is a missionary disciple (agent of evangelization). Confirm.

Unity note: Acts 17:26, 'of one, all mankind', is used as the day's one-human-family line, from Paul's own speech; Paul's opening from the Athenians' altar and poets is presented as the model for sharing faith gently. The poet quoted in 17:28 is often identified as Aratus; not named in the voice.
'Waiting for friends to catch up' rests on Acts 17:16 (Paul waiting for Silas and Timothy).
Shape: story (Paul in Athens, after the end of Mass). Practice kind: text someone (writing it is the practice; sending is optional).
